newsitem.title: KENYA: Ethiopian pilot speaks of hijack ordeal.
newsitem.headline: Ethiopian pilot speaks of hijack ordeal.

text.p: The pilot of the Ethiopian Airlines Boeing 767 that crashed into the Indian ocean last week recounted on Friday his terrifying ordeal as fuel steadily ran out while the three hijackers insisted on flying to Australia.
Captain Leul Abate, 42, one of 50 survivors, told Reuters from his bed in a Nairobi hospital how the men stormed the flight deck after take-off from Addis Ababa last Saturday.

"When the hijackers got into the cockpit they started shouting, beat up the co-pilot and threw him out. They said: 'We want to go to Australia, otherwise we will blow the plane up... We know this is a 767 and it can fly for 11 hours'," the Ethiopian pilot said.
The hijackers at first ignored his attempts, helped by air traffic controllers in the Kenyan city of Mombasa, to persuade them he needed to refuel before going to Australia.
"I and Mombasa air control explained that it was not possible and the plane would have to make stops," Leul added.
"After some argument I think they understood we could not go to Australia (without stops)." But they nevertheless refused to land at Mombasa.

"Fuel running out? They knew about it because I was showing them the fuel gauges. One engine flared out. He (the main hijacker of the two inside the cockpit) was refusing, not to descend. I was doing it on my own."
The hijackers realised Leul was hugging the coast heading south and told him to head east across the Indian Ocean. He made for the Indian ocean islands of Comoros.
The hijackers, who spoke Ethiopia's Amharic language and French amongst themselves, warned Leul not to go below 39,000 feet.
As the pilot went below 25,000, one of the hijackers said: "If you go any lower we will blow up the plane."

"I said: "Listen, guys, we're all dead people, there is no argument now. He (the main hijacker) was struggling, interfering with the controls. He went back to the (first class) cabin, so I was trying to fly it all the way down. In the last two minutes my first officer rushed into the cockpit and he assisted me in the final ditching of the airplane," Leul added.

The hijackers told Leul they had a bomb and threatened to blow up the airliner unless he did as told. One of the hijackers was brandishing an axe and two of them were drinking whisky on the flight deck throughout the episode.

The hijackers never told the pilot their motive apart from saying they wanted to go and seek political asylum in Australia. They are believed to have died in the crash but this has not been confirmed officially.

On Thursday another survivor, Monica Tibwitta, told Reuters that award-winning Kenyan cameraman Mohamed "Mo" Amin, one for the 125 killed in the crash, was negotiating with the hijackers in the minutes before the Boeing crashed into the sea.

Tibwitta said Amin, with either one or two other passengers in the plane's first-class section, stood up shortly after Leul told passengers he had virtually no more fuel and they should prepare for a crash landing.

"I remember when the pilot announced about the emergency landing, he (Amin) stood up and started talking to the hijackers and tried to negotiate with them," Tibwitta said by telephone from her bed in the private Nairobi Hospital.
